"DEATH-BOARDS" in the Bavarian Forest.

In the Eastern half of Bavaria, touching the Kingdom of Bohemia, lies the so-called Bavarian Forest which - speaking geographically - is only a spur of the large and mountainous Bahemian Forest. This part of the country, although abundant in beautiful sceneries, is almost devoid of visitors and tourists, probably for the reason that the charms of this region, owing to the lack of advertising, are too little known even in Germany, - on the other hand the hotel and boarding accomodations which are usually encountered there, are far from giving satisfaction even to an ardent advocate of the "simple life " theory. This part of Bavaria has been in many ways untouched by civilisation and owing to its seclusion from the outer world, some very strange customs are still in vague which strongly remind one of the Middle Ages. One of these strange customs there, strictly observed by the population, is the way in which they keep awake the memory of their dead by the erection of what they call "TOTENBRETTER ", or "DEAT BOARDS". They are wooden boards cut in the shape of tomb-stones and roughly painted (sometimes bearing also the image of a Saint and they are erected, often in a row of 30 and more, on the roadside, in fields and meadows, near chapels and crucifixes, in the village streets, shortly everywhere, and they are even nailed to houses and barns. They do not - which must be emphasized - signify any burial places, but as soon as a person has died, the corpse is put on a board and there it lies in state until it is put into the coffin shortly before the funeral. These boards, then, are the so-called DEATH-BOARDS. After the funeral they are cut into a suitable shape and they are given an inscription containing the name of the deceased who has been lying on it, his age and in most cases also some lines in poetry. These short poems which are, of course, meant in good earnest, are sometimes very amusing, but the cannot be translated as their funny side lies in the dialect in which they are perpetrated. These boards are then stuck somewhere near the road, or in the fields where they sometimes accumulate to an alarming number. In poorer districts these boards are not alway cut into shape and painted, but they are, in their natural state, simply deposited at the foot of some crucifix where they remain, untouched for ever, until they moulder away. It must be admitted that this custom, strange as it may be, seems rather objectionable from a hygienic point of view, nor is it very exhilarating for the tourist to be reminded of death wherever he may put his feet.

A German New-Year Custom: Lead Casting.

On New-Year's eve the members of the family use to assemble around a table to indulge in the old custom of lead casting which is an old German superstition. In a tin ladle small pieces of lead are melted over the flame of a candle or the like, and the lead when molten, is rapidly poured into a bowl with cold water. Very queer formations are the result, and from the shape of them - which is of course mere guesswork in which individual fancy has a large field - people try to distinguish some objects, be it a flower, or a gun, or a coffin, or a cradle etc. etc. These objects, then, are supposed to be a sign of what the future year will bring.
